subject: Integration ops walkthrough: SDK auth, routing, req/resp schema & streaming semantics
messages:
From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>
To: Samira Khan <samira@lumenai.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 03 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Integration ops walkthrough: SDK auth, routing, req/resp schema & streaming semantics

Hi Samira / Miguel,

Great to meet today — thanks for the time. Quick post-call recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment on integration expectations and the remaining decision points for the pilot. Attaching a simple auth diagram and a short req/resp example doc.

Summary of what we covered:
- Primary integration path: client app -> Redwood SDK (JS/Python) -> Redwood runtime (hosted) -> model variants (routing by latency/cost).
- Key capabilities you want: streaming partials in the UI, tool-calling / structured JSON outputs, embeddings for reranking, and predictable token billing.
- Constraints: need short-lived credentials for delegates, reranker must run within 300ms at P95, and we must enforce stop token behavior client-side for customer-facing content.

Open questions we promised to answer this week (please confirm priority):
1) SDK auth patterns: recommend short-lived JWTs via your backend vs long-lived API keys?
2) Streaming semantics: how to emit partial tokens vs finalization events; how stop tokens and max_tokens interact.
3) Req/resp schema: chat vs completions model choices for structured tool-calling and JSON schema enforcement.
4) Embeddings/reranker flow: top-k dense retrieval -> rerank approach and tokenization effects.

Next steps we propose:
- Karthik to provide a concise technical note answering 1–4 with code snippets and a recommended default configuration for a pilot.
- Ben to schedule a 30-minute ops sync next Wed to confirm infra and SLAs.
- You (Samira) to confirm which environments (staging / prod) you want reserved for pilot traffic.

Attachments: redwood-sdk-auth-flow.png (auth diagram), reqresp-examples.md (req/resp snippets and examples).

Thanks again — will leave the technical follow-up to Karthik but happy to jump on call if any of these answers need more context.

Best,
Evelyn Hart
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Integration ops walkthrough: SDK auth, routing, req/resp schema & streaming semantics

Thanks Evelyn — helpful recap. A few clarifying questions before Karthik's note so we get the right level of detail: 

1) Auth: we prefer not to embed long-lived keys in the client. For the pilot, do you recommend (A) our backend minting short-lived API tokens for the client via Redwood's token exchange, or (B) using our OIDC provider and configuring Redwood as a relying party? Any gotchas around token refresh under high concurrency?

2) Streaming vs finalization: our UX team wants to show token-level typing (progressive partials) but block rendering until the structured JSON is valid (tool-calls). How do you recommend signaling the UI that a JSON tool call is complete vs still streaming?

3) Stop tokens + max_tokens: if we set max_tokens=150 and a stop token is encountered earlier, is the token consumption billed to the stop token or to max_tokens? Also: will streaming end immediately on the stop token or do we risk partial JSON fragments?

4) Embeddings/rerank: we currently do dense retrieval (FAISS) and then call a cross-encoder re-ranker. Do you suggest running the reranker inside Redwood as a second model call (costly) or doing local cross-encoder re-rank? Latency target is <300ms P95 for the rerank stage.

If you can cover those specifically it will help our product and infra folks.

Samira
Head of Product | Lumen AI

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Samira Khan <samira@lumenai.com>
Cc: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 03 Sep 2026 17:40:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Integration ops walkthrough: SDK auth, routing, req/resp schema & streaming semantics

Hi Samira — answering each point with recommended defaults for the pilot plus rationale. Longer form notes attached (reqresp-examples.md) and I dropped a simplified auth flow PNG in the thread.

1) Auth (recommendation):
- Default: your backend mints short-lived tokens (15m–1h) via Redwood's token-exchange endpoint. This minimizes long-lived keys in the client and keeps issuer control on your side.
- OIDC option: supported for enterprise customers (we can federate via your IdP). Note: OIDC adds an extra round-trip during initial handshake and requires your IdP to support client-assertion flows for good concurrency behavior.
- Concurrency: if you do high QPS token minting, use a token caching layer on your backend keyed by user-session to avoid thundering herd on Redwood's token-exchange; tokens are cheap to issue but still add latency.

2) Streaming semantics & tool-calling (structured JSON):
- Pattern: stream all partials to the UI as "delta" events, but emit a separate finalization event when the model completes a valid JSON object per the provided JSON schema.
- Implementation detail: send streaming token deltas on the WebSocket/http chunk. Our runtime supports an explicit "event: finalized" frame when the output validates against the schema you provided in the request (we validate incrementally but only mark finalized when JSON is syntactically valid and schema checks pass).
- Practical UX approach: show progressive typing for human-readable fields; for tool-calls, render a loading placeholder for the tool payload until you receive the finalized event. This avoids executing incomplete JSON.

3) Stop tokens vs max_tokens (billing and truncation):
- Billing: charges are based on tokens processed by the model (input + model-output tokens). If the model emits a stop token, the emitted stop token itself counts toward tokens consumed only if it is actually emitted. If stop prevents emission (model suppresses token), it's not charged as output. In practice assume stop tokens are inexpensive relative to overall output.
- max_tokens: enforces an upper bound on output tokens; the runtime will truncate/stop generation when max_tokens reached regardless of stop tokens. If a stop token is encountered earlier, generation stops and we emit a finalization event.
- Streaming behavior: streaming stops as soon as the model halts (stop token or max_tokens). We do some post-processing to ensure the last chunk doesn't cut a UTF-8 boundary or break JSON tokenization; however, there is a small window where partial JSON fragments could be streamed before the finalization event — hence the finalization event is the reliable signal to parse/execute tool-calls.

4) Embeddings and rerank (latency tradeoffs):
- Recommendation: hybrid approach for the pilot: do dense retrieval (FAISS) on your side to get top-N candidates (N=100), send top-10 to Redwood reranker endpoint (cross-encoder hosted) if you need best-quality re-rank within a predictable SLA. This keeps the heavy cross-encoder close to inference infra and simplifies tokenization consistency.
- If you need <300ms P95 and cost is a concern, run a lightweight local cross-encoder for the first pass and use Redwood cross-encoder as an async re-rank for offline metrics/quality checks.
- Embeddings caveat: ensure you use the same tokenizer/normalization for your FAISS index as Redwood's embedding encoder to avoid drift. We expose a model-specific tokenizer spec in the SDK.

5) Req/resp schema: chat vs completions
- Use chat-style API for multi-turn interactions and when you want system/user/assistant role separation. Chat API also better supports function/tool-calling primitives with explicit JSON schemas.
- Completions-style calls are fine for single-shot generation and simpler cost models, but tool-calling is less ergonomic.

SDK example (JS, minimal)
```
import Redwood from '@redwood/inference-js'
const client = new Redwood({ token: '<short-lived-token>' })
// stream example
const ev = client.chat.stream({
  model: 'rwd-chat-large',
  messages: [{ role: 'system', content: 'You are an assistant.' }, { role: 'user', content: 'Generate JSON for tool-call' }],
  schema: { type: 'object', properties: { action: { type: 'string' }, payload: { type: 'object' } }, required: ['action'] },
  stream: true,
  max_output_tokens: 150,
  stop: ['
---STOP---']
})
ev.on('delta', chunk => /* render partial */)
ev.on('finalized', json => /* execute tool with validated json */)
```

Operational notes:
- Routing: start with latency-first routing for the pilot, with automatic fallback to cheaper quantized variants if latency SLA cannot be met.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching works best when session IDs are stable; recommend hashing session_id + conversation_id as cache key.
- Tokenization: client should guard total token budget (input + expected output). We provide tokenization utilities in the SDK.

Attachments: reqresp-examples.md (contains explicit chat/completions examples, token accounting table, and sample JSON schemas), redwood-sdk-auth-flow.png (auth flow).

If that looks good I'll create a trimmed config you can drop into your staging build. Happy to hop on a 20m technical deep-dive.

-Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Thanks Karthik — super helpful and concrete. A couple quick notes from our side:
- We'll start with backend-minted 30m tokens and add a small token cache layer to avoid burst minting.
- UX will implement progressive UI for text and only enable the tool execution on your "finalized" event (this matches what we wanted).
- For rerank: we'll prototype local lightweight cross-encoder first and call Redwood's re-ranker for smoke tests / offline evals while we profile latency.

Can you share the small pilot config file you mentioned and a suggested list of model variants for latency-first routing? If you can drop the config to the Drive link in your note, we'll pick a staging date this week.

Samira
Head of Product | Lumen AI
